title: Crossmap Explorer
text:
A companion to xmap’s vignettes and to the crossmaps definition paper (Huang 2024, arXiv:2406.14163), extending the “exploratory power of a crossmap collection” idea onto the full, real INDSTAT Rev.3 extract – using isiccomb combination-code splitting as a running case study. See CLAUDE.md for the full architecture writeup.
This site is deliberately a linear set of Quarto notebooks, not a data pipeline with a build tool behind it: Extraction runs the vignette’s naive-weight extraction technique once and saves a single crossmap_collection.rds artifact; every other page just reads that file.

Extraction – the naive-weight (“carbon paper”) extraction + per-country-year validation, on real data
Coverage – which country-years rely on a split at all, and how much
Explorer – zoom into one country-year’s isiccomb -> isic -> isic.3 crossmap as a node-link diagram
Country variants – all the structurally distinct crossmaps a single country used over time
Composed overview – the whole-classification isiccomb -> isic.3 structure, composed via xmap::compose_xmap()

title: Country Variants
text:
Explorer picks any single country-year from the globally-deduplicated list of 218 distinct crossmap patterns. This page asks a different question: for one country, how many genuinely different isiccomb -> isic crossmaps did it use across all its reporting years, and when did each apply?
A country’s classification/reporting scheme is not always fixed over time – e.g. DEU (Germany, code 276) turns out to have used 3 structurally distinct crossmaps across its 13 reporting years, not 13 independent ones. This groups a single country’s years by identical crossmap signature – the same de-duplication as the Explorer page, just sliced by country first instead of pooled across all countries.

## within each country, collapse years sharing an identical crossmap
## signature into one "variant" -- year_range covers all years using
## that variant, first_year is the representative used to pull edges
## for the diagram (every year in the group has the same edges by
## construction, so any one of them will do)
country_variants <- ctr_year_signature |>
  group_by(country, name, signature) |>
  summarise(
    year_range = collapse_years(year),
    n_yr = n(),
    first_year = min(year),
    n_combo = n_combo[1],
    n_crossing = n_crossing[1],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(country, first_year) |>
  mutate(variant_label = paste0(
    year_range, "  [", n_combo, " isiccomb, ", n_crossing, " crossing, ", n_yr, " yr]"
  ))

title: Country Variants
Split Coverage
text:
Two different questions, at two different stages of the transformation:

Stage 1 (below): was this isic value touched by an isiccomb split at all? This only looks at isiccomb -> isic in isolation – it has no notion of isic.3 and can’t distinguish a split that’s harmless from one that isn’t.
Stage 1+2 (further below): composing the split with the deterministic isic -> isic.3 aggregation, does the combined transformation actually cross an isic.3 boundary? A split whose children all reconverge into the same isic.3 parent is imputed at the 4-digit level but exact at 3-digit and coarser (the 1/n weights cancel out on re-aggregation); a split whose children land in different isic.3 parents carries real, propagated allocation uncertainty. Only the second kind should really count as “consequential” imputation exposure. This is the same distinction the node-link diagrams in Explorer/ Country variants show per component (a reconvergent vs. diverging fan of dashed split edges); this page shows its coverage-level rollup.

title: Split Coverage
text:
Setup
Reads the crossmap collection prepared by Extraction – render that page first if data/interim/crossmap_collection.rds is missing or stale.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(here)




Code
crossmap_collection <- readRDS(here("data", "interim", "crossmap_collection.rds"))
tile_any_split <- crossmap_collection$tile_any_split
tile_frac_split <- crossmap_collection$tile_frac_split
tile_frac_split_crossing <- crossmap_collection$tile_frac_split_crossing
ctr_codes <- crossmap_collection$ctr_codes


All three tiles below share one country ordering – by each country’s overall (all-years-pooled) fraction of isic values in a crossing component, weighted by volume (sum(n_crossing) / sum(n_isic), not a plain per-year average, so a country’s one thin reporting year can’t skew its rank) – rather than each plot re-sorting on its own metric. That keeps a given row meaning “this country” consistently across all three figures, so you can read the same row down the page and see stage-1 coverage vs. stage-1+2 consequential coverage for the same country side by side.


Code
country_order <- tile_frac_split_crossing |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(total_isic = sum(n_isic), total_crossing = sum(n_crossing), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(agg_frac_crossing = total_crossing / total_isic) |>
  arrange(agg_frac_crossing) |>
  pull(country)

title: Split Coverage
text:
Stage 1: Split Coverage (isiccomb -> isic)
Two views of the same underlying fact, at different resolutions: the binary tile is a strict coarsening of the continuous one (any_split == (frac_split > 0)) – read them as a pair, binary for “where does this even come up,” continuous for “how much does it matter there.”

Any Split?


Code
tile_any_split |>
  left_join(ctr_codes, by = c("country" = "code")) |>
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = country_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(year), y = country, fill = any_split)) +
  geom_tile(color = "black") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = ~ str_sub(.x, -2)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#ef8a62", "FALSE" = "#67a9cf")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", y = "Country", fill = "Any split?",
    title = "Countries reporting isiccomb combination codes",
    subtitle = "INDSTAT 4 REV. 3 Output data -- stage 1 only"
  )











Fraction Split


Code
tile_frac_split |>
  left_join(ctr_codes, by = c("country" = "code")) |>
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = country_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(year), y = country, fill = frac_split)) +
  geom_tile(color = "black") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = ~ str_sub(.x, -2)) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", y = "Country", fill = "Fraction split",
    title = "Share of isic values derived from an isiccomb split",
    subtitle = "INDSTAT 4 REV. 3 Output data -- stage 1 only"
  )

title: Split Coverage
Split Coverage
text:
Biggest Overstatements
Aggregating (all years pooled, volume-weighted – same approach as country_order above) down to one row per country makes it possible to ask directly: for which reporters is stage-1 frac_split mostly noise (reconvergent diamonds), and for which is it mostly signal (genuine crossing)? Restricted to countries with at least 5 split rows pooled across all their years, so a single small sample can’t produce a misleadingly clean 0% or 100%.


Code
country_split_summary <- tile_frac_split |>
  left_join(tile_frac_split_crossing |> select(country, year, n_crossing),
    by = c("country", "year")
  ) |>
  left_join(ctr_codes, by = c("country" = "code")) |>
  group_by(country, name) |>
  summarise(
    n_years = n(),
    total_split = sum(n_split),
    total_crossing = sum(n_crossing),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    total_reconverging = total_split - total_crossing,
    pct_split_reconverging = 100 * total_reconverging / total_split
  ) |>
  filter(total_split >= 5)


Ranked by absolute overstatement: how much stage-1 coverage this country would report vs. how much of that is actually consequential (largest gap first – i.e. the countries where looking only at the first tile above would mislead you the most):


Code
country_split_summary |>
  left_join(
    tile_frac_split |> group_by(country) |> summarise(total_isic = sum(n_isic), .groups = "drop"),
    by = "country"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    frac_split = total_split / total_isic,
    frac_crossing = total_crossing / total_isic,
    gap = frac_split - frac_crossing
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(gap)) |>
  transmute(
    country, name, n_years, total_split, total_reconverging,
    pct_split_reconverging = round(pct_split_reconverging, 1),
    frac_split = round(frac_split, 3),
    frac_crossing = round(frac_crossing, 3),
    gap = round(gap, 3)
  ) |>
  head(15) |>
  knitr::kable()

title: Extracting the Crossmap Collection
text:
This page is a companion to xmap’s vignette extracting-crossmaps-from-scripts.Rmd (specifically Case 2, PR #4) – it runs the same “carbon paper” naive-weight extraction technique end to end on the full, real INDSTAT Rev.3 extract (all reporters and years, not the vignette’s 5-country masked-sample subset), and saves the result as a single artifact the rest of this site reads from.
The technique, restated: rather than trusting or parsing a legacy data-cleaning script’s logic directly, pass “simplified” (masked) data through it and recover the mapping it implies from the output. This works even when the real values are sensitive, since only the structure of the transform – which source codes map to which targets, at what weight – is being recovered, not the real data.
Every other page in this site loads data/interim/crossmap_collection.rds, produced at the end of this page, rather than recomputing any of this. There is no build-system dependency graph (no targets/_targets.R) – this is deliberately a single, linear, readable extraction notebook, in keeping with this site’s purpose as a companion to the vignette and to the crossmaps definition paper, not a general-purpose data pipeline. If you change this page’s logic, re-render it before the other pages, or just quarto render the whole project (files are numbered so this one sorts and renders first).

Raw Extract

read_rev3_output <- function(file) {
  readr::read_csv(file,
    col_types = readr::cols(
      ctable = readr::col_double(),
      country = readr::col_character(),

text:
Validation
A crossmap collection is many small crossmaps stacked in one table, so validity has to be checked within each (country, year) group, not across the whole table at once:


Code
diagnoses_isiccomb_isic <- diagnose_grouped_xmap(links_isiccomb_isic, isiccomb, isic, weight)

diagnoses_isiccomb_isic |> count(valid)


# A tibble: 1 × 2

  <lgl> <int>
1 TRUE   1523

title: Extracting the Crossmap Collection
Extracting the Crossmap Collection
text:
Composing isiccomb -> isic.3 (d)
xmap#29 shipped xmap::compose_xmap(), so the two crossmaps above – the split (isiccomb -> isic) and the deterministic aggregation (isic -> isic.3) – can now be chained through their shared isic intermediate directly, instead of the placeholder page that used to wait on it:


Code
xmap2_isic_isic3 <- links_isic_isic3 |>
  as_xmap_tbl(isic, isic3, weight_by = weight)

composed_isiccomb_isic3 <- compose_grouped_xmap(
  links_isiccomb_isic, xmap2_isic_isic3, isiccomb, isic, weight
)

composed_isiccomb_isic3

Every isiccomb code turns out to have exactly one composed (isic3, weight) signature everywhere it’s reported – i.e. no code splits differently in one country-year than another – so the composed collection dedups down to the whole-classification structure with no extra reconciliation step, exactly as anticipated when (d) was still blocked:


Code
composed_isiccomb_isic3 |>
  dplyr::distinct(country, year, isiccomb, isic3, weight) |>
  dplyr::arrange(isiccomb, isic3) |>
  dplyr::group_by(isiccomb) |>
  dplyr::summarise(sig = paste(isic3, round(weight, 6), sep = "=", collapse = ";"), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::group_by(isiccomb) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_variants = dplyr::n_distinct(sig), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::count(n_variants)


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_variants     n
       <int> <int>
1          1   457


Composed overview uses this to build the deduplicated global overview: distinct (isiccomb, isic3, weight) triples, bundling away one-to-one (non-splitting, non-aggregating) codes and showing only the codes that cross an isic.3 boundary.

dir.create(here("data", "interim"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

  links_isiccomb_isic = links_isiccomb_isic,
  links_isic_isic3 = links_isic_isic3,
  diagnoses_isiccomb_isic = diagnoses_isiccomb_isic,
  tile_any_split = tile_any_split,
  tile_frac_split = tile_frac_split,
  tile_frac_split_crossing = tile_frac_split_crossing,
  combo_edges = combo_edges,
  comb_group_span = comb_group_span,
  comb_code_span = comb_code_span,
  ctr_year_signature = ctr_year_signature,
  max_isic3_indegree = max_isic3_indegree,
  composed_isiccomb_isic3 = composed_isiccomb_isic3
)

saveRDS(crossmap_collection, here("data", "interim", "crossmap_collection.rds"))

title: Country-Year Explorer
text:
Component (c): zoom into a single country-year’s crossmap collection. (Component (d), the whole-classification overview, is a separate page – see Composed overview, built on xmap::compose_xmap(), xmap#29.)
Node-link crossmap design from Huang (2023), arxiv:2308.06535 – the design behind the xmap package itself – rather than a Sankey diagram:

source node text: italic for one-to-many (splitting) sources, bold for one-to-one sources
edge line style: dashed for one-to-many splits, solid for one-to-one relations, instead of Sankey’s ribbon-width-as-weight
edge weight labels: shown as text on the edge; dropped on solid (one-to-one) edges to reduce clutter, since that weight just repeats the incoming split edge’s label
target node shading: opacity/color scaled by in-degree (# of incoming edges), to show how “synthetic” a target category is

This is a 3-column chained node-link diagram per isiccomb code: isiccomb -> isic member -> isic.3 parent, combining two crossmaps (the split, and the 3-vs-4-digit aggregation) into one figure, since the middle column (isic) is simultaneously the target of the first crossmap and the source of the second.

Setup

Code
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("R", "prep.R")) # collapse_years()




Code
crossmap_collection <- readRDS(here("data", "interim", "crossmap_collection.rds"))
combo_edges <- crossmap_collection$combo_edges
ctr_year_signature <- crossmap_collection$ctr_year_signature
max_isic3_indegree <- crossmap_collection$max_isic3_indegree

title: Country-Year Explorer
text:
Preparing the Diagram
Many country-years share the exact same isiccomb crossmap structure (e.g. the same reporter using the same national classification variant for a run of consecutive years). Rendering one diagram per country-year would repeat identical figures dozens of times, so we first collapse country-years into groups that share an identical crossmap (same set of isiccomb -> isic edges with the same weights) and show each distinct pattern only once, labelled with which country-years share it.
This groups across countries – see Country variants instead for “all the variants a single country used over time” (e.g. all the crossmaps DEU has had).


Code
## group country-years sharing an identical signature; one representative
## (country, year) per group is enough to render the diagram, since every
## member of the group has the same edges by construction
crossmap_group_list <- ctr_year_signature |>
  group_by(signature) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    by_ctr <- .x |>
      group_by(country, name) |>
      summarise(year_range = collapse_years(year), n_yr = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
      arrange(desc(n_yr))
    tibble(
      country = .x$country[1],
      year = .x$year[1],
      n_combo = .x$n_combo[1],
      n_crossing = .x$n_crossing[1],
      n_ctryr = nrow(.x),
      detail = paste(paste0(by_ctr$name, " (", by_ctr$country, "): ", by_ctr$year_range), collapse = "; ")
    )
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(desc(n_crossing), desc(n_combo), desc(n_ctryr)) |>
  mutate(label = paste0(
    "[", n_combo, " isiccomb, ", n_crossing, " crossing, ", n_ctryr, " country-yrs] ", detail
  ))

crossmap_group_list |> select(-signature)

Composed Overview
text:
Component (d): the composed, whole-classification isiccomb -> isic.3 view – one graph, not per country-year, showing every place in the classification where a real one-to-many split or many-to-one aggregation happens, with the pass-through-unchanged majority collapsed out of view.
Composed with xmap::compose_xmap() in Extraction, chaining isiccomb -> isic and isic -> isic.3 through their shared isic intermediate into a single isiccomb -> isic.3 crossmap – without materialising isic-level values, which aren’t meaningful on their own (they’re an artifact of the naive split). This is the same information Explorer/ Country variants show per country-year component, at the whole-classification level: not “what happened in one country-year” but “which isiccomb codes, anywhere in the dataset, actually carry a real split or aggregation.”

title: Composed Overview
text:
Setup
Reads the crossmap collection prepared by Extraction – render that page first if data/interim/crossmap_collection.rds is missing or stale.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("R", "prep.R")) # collapse_years()




Code
crossmap_collection <- readRDS(here("data", "interim", "crossmap_collection.rds"))
composed_isiccomb_isic3 <- crossmap_collection$composed_isiccomb_isic3
ctr_codes <- crossmap_collection$ctr_codes

title: Composed Overview
text:
Preparing the Diagram
Every isiccomb code turns out to compose the exact same way in every country-year that reports it (see Extraction), so the composed crossmap collapses to one global structure with no extra reconciliation – distinct (isiccomb, isic3, weight) triples, bundling away the pass-through-unchanged majority (a code mapping to exactly one isic.3 parent at weight 1) and showing only codes that cross an isic.3 boundary.


Code
## dedup: every isiccomb code composes identically in every country-year
## that reports it, so a global distinct() is a lossless reduction
composed_code_edges <- composed_isiccomb_isic3 |>
  distinct(isiccomb, isic3, weight) |>
  add_count(isiccomb, name = "n_isic3")

n_codes <- n_distinct(composed_code_edges$isiccomb)
n_bundled <- composed_code_edges |> filter(n_isic3 == 1) |> nrow()
n_crossing <- n_codes - n_bundled

composed_crossing_edges <- composed_code_edges |>
  filter(n_isic3 > 1) |>
  arrange(desc(n_isic3), isiccomb)

glue::glue(
  "{n_codes} distinct isiccomb codes in the classification: ",
  "{n_bundled} map one-to-one onto a single isic.3 parent (bundled, not shown below); ",
  "{n_crossing} cross into more than one isic.3 parent."
)


457 distinct isiccomb codes in the classification: 278 map one-to-one onto a single isic.3 parent (bundled, not shown below); 179 cross into more than one isic.3 parent.


Deduping away country/year above is lossless for the structure of each component, but it also erases which slice of the real dataset each small multiple actually reflects – a code reported by one country in one year and a code reported by 50 country-years look identical otherwise. Same country-year attribution as crossmap_group_list’s detail field in Explorer, computed here per isiccomb instead of per identical-crossmap group:
coverage_summary caps the always-visible subtitle at the top 3 countries by years reported (+N more beyond that) – codes reported by dozens of countries (e.g. 1810A, 45 countries) would otherwise produce a ~1300-character subtitle wrapping across a whole small multiple. coverage_detail (full, untruncated) is kept for the hover tooltip.


Code
composed_code_coverage <- composed_isiccomb_isic3 |>
  distinct(country, year, isiccomb) |>
  semi_join(composed_crossing_edges, by = "isiccomb") |>
  left_join(ctr_codes, by = c("country" = "code")) |>
  group_by(isiccomb, country, name) |>
  summarise(year_range = collapse_years(year), n_yr = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(isiccomb, desc(n_yr)) |>
  group_by(isiccomb) |>
  summarise(
    n_country = n_distinct(country),
    n_ctryr = sum(n_yr),
    coverage_detail = paste(paste0(name, " (", country, "): ", year_range), collapse = "; "),
    coverage_summary = {
      entries <- paste0(name, " (", country, "): ", year_range)
      shown <- entries[seq_len(min(3, length(entries)))]
      n_more <- length(entries) - length(shown)
      if (n_more > 0) paste0(paste(shown, collapse = "; "), "; +", n_more, " more")
      else paste(shown, collapse = "; ")
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  )
